Defective mineralisation of growing bone (the growth plate and the osteoid) in children.
What is the same defect called after the growth plates have closed?
Where is 25-hydroxyvitamin D converted to the active form?
In the kidney, by 1α-hydroxylase, which is stimulated by parathyroid hormone (PTH).
What is the best test of vitamin D status?
Which 25-hydroxyvitamin D level defines vitamin D deficiency?
What is the most common cause of rickets?
Nutritional rickets: vitamin D deficiency and/or a low calcium intake.
What is the peak age of nutritional rickets?
Why does an exclusively breastfed infant develop rickets without supplements?
Breast milk is low in vitamin D.
Phenytoin and phenobarbitone speed up the breakdown of vitamin D.
What is the defect in vitamin D-dependent rickets type 1?
Absent renal 1α-hydroxylase, so the level of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is low.
What is the clue to vitamin D-dependent rickets type 2?
Alopecia with a very high 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D level, because of resistance of the vitamin D receptor.
What is the commonest inherited form of rickets?
X-linked hypophosphataemic rickets: the kidney loses phosphate and the PTH is normal.
What is the earliest clinical sign of rickets in a young infant?
Craniotabes: a soft skull that yields like a ping-pong ball.
Rounded, painless swelling of the costochondral junctions.
A groove of the lower chest along the attachment of the diaphragm.
What are the fontanelle and head findings in rickets?
A wide, late-closing anterior fontanelle, with frontal and parietal bossing.
Which leg deformity appears after the child walks?
Bow legs (genu varum), and later knock knees.
What are the muscle and motor signs of rickets?
Hypotonia, delayed motor milestones and a pot belly.
How does the rosary of scurvy differ from the rosary of rickets?
In scurvy it is sharp, angular and tender; in rickets it is rounded and painless.
What is the biochemistry of nutritional rickets?
Calcium normal or low, phosphate low, alkaline phosphatase (ALP) and PTH high, and 25-hydroxyvitamin D low.
What is the best blood marker of rickets activity and healing?
Which finding is NOT consistent with nutritional rickets?
A raised serum phosphate, which is seen in chronic kidney disease.
Why is the serum calcium often normal in rickets?
The raised PTH mobilises calcium from bone (and makes the kidney lose phosphate).
What are the X-ray signs of active rickets at the wrist?
A widened, cupped and frayed metaphysis with low bone density.
What is the first X-ray sign of healing?
A dense white line of calcification at the metaphysis, 2–4 weeks after vitamin D is started.
What is the biochemistry of X-linked hypophosphataemic rickets?
A very low phosphate, with normal calcium and normal PTH.
What daily vitamin D treatment is given to a 2-year-old with rickets?
3000–6000 IU daily for 12 weeks, together with calcium 500 mg daily.
What daily vitamin D treatment is given under 12 months of age?
2000 IU daily for 12 weeks, together with calcium.
What is the single oral (stoss) dose of vitamin D for children aged 1–12 years?
When daily drops are unlikely to be taken. It is not used under 3 months of age.
What calcium dose is given with vitamin D treatment?
How is hypocalcaemic tetany or a hypocalcaemic seizure treated in an emergency?
10% calcium gluconate 0.5 ml/kg intravenously (maximum 20 ml) over 10 minutes, with cardiac monitoring.
What is the drug of choice in vitamin D-dependent rickets?
How is X-linked hypophosphataemic rickets treated?
Oral phosphate with calcitriol, or burosumab.
When is healing checked, and how?
At 3 months, with the ALP and a wrist X-ray.
How much vitamin D is given to prevent rickets in infancy?
400 IU daily from birth to 12 months, however the baby is fed.
What are the features of vitamin D toxicity?
Hypercalcaemia: vomiting, constipation, polyuria and nephrocalcinosis.
What is the main action of active vitamin D on the gut?
It increases the absorption of calcium and phosphate from the small intestine.
What are the effects of PTH on the kidney?
It increases calcium reabsorption, decreases phosphate reabsorption (phosphaturia) and increases 1α-hydroxylase activity.
Why is the phosphate low in nutritional rickets?
The low calcium raises PTH, which makes the kidney lose phosphate.
